content.content:
1	Many liquid handling installations add a small, accurately measured quantity of a concentrate to a much larger stream of a carrier liquid that is already flowing in a pipe. The concentrate may be aggressive, staining, strongly coloured, biologically active, or simply expensive, and the quantity that must be added is small in comparison with the carrier flow. The addition therefore has to be made repeatably, without measuring the concentrate by eye, and without allowing the concentrate to reach any part of the installation other than the carrier stream itself.
2	
3	Two practical difficulties dominate this kind of dosing. The first is separation of the two liquids upstream of the point of addition. A dosing device sits between a concentrate source and a pressurised carrier line, and any path that momentarily connects the two allows carrier liquid to be forced back into the concentrate source or allows concentrate to migrate into the carrier line at a time when no dose is called for. Devices that rely on separately actuated shut-off elements to keep the two sides apart depend on those elements being commanded in the correct order, so a control fault, a lost signal, or a slow-acting element can open both sides at once.
4	
5	The second difficulty is residue. The surfaces that the concentrate touches, in particular the port through which it enters the metering volume and the seat of the check element through which the dose leaves, retain a film of concentrate after the dose has been delivered. That film drips into the carrier stream between doses, so the quantity actually added is not the quantity that was measured. It also dries, crystallises, or reacts on the wetted surfaces, so that a valve which was accurate when new drifts, sticks, or seizes in service. The usual remedy is to break the valve out of the line and clean it by hand, which takes the installation out of service and exposes the person doing the work to the concentrate. Where a rinse is provided at all, it is commonly a separate operation that has to be commanded after the dose, and it therefore depends on an operator or a controller performing an extra step at the right moment.
6	
7	Dose selection presents a further difficulty. Adjustable dosing devices are often set by a screw or by an electronically stored value. A screw setting can be lost during cleaning and gives no indication of what was set. An electronic setting requires power, a sensor and a display at the valve, which is unwelcome in wet, washdown or hazardous locations, and it tells the operator only what the controller believes rather than what the mechanism will actually deliver.
8	
9	There remains a need for an inline metering valve in which the separation of the concentrate from the carrier liquid is enforced by the geometry of the moving parts rather than by the order in which external commands arrive, in which the surfaces wetted by the concentrate are rinsed by the carrier liquid as an unavoidable part of the return of the metering element, and in which the selected dose is both retained and displayed mechanically.
10

1	In the following description, the terms upstream and downstream refer to the direction of travel of the carrier liquid from the inlet toward the outlet, and the terms axial and radial refer to the axis along which the piston slides.
2	
3	FIG. 1 shows an inline liquid metering valve 10 having a cylindrical housing 12 with an inlet 14 at one axial end and an outlet 16 at the opposite axial end, a metering sleeve 18 fixed within the housing 12, a cartridge 64 retained in the housing 12 by a threaded end cap 66, and a transparent window 52 in the housing 12.
4	
5	The inline liquid metering valve 10 is connected in a line that already carries a flowing carrier liquid. Carrier liquid enters at the inlet 14, passes along the housing 12, and leaves at the outlet 16. That flow is the main flow into which each dose of concentrate is delivered, and it is also the only liquid used to rinse the valve. The metering sleeve 18 is spaced radially inward from the inner surface of the housing 12 over part of its length.
6	
7	FIG. 2 shows the metering sleeve 18 defining a dose chamber 20, a concentrate port 22 opening into the dose chamber 20 and a carrier-liquid admission port 24 opening into the dose chamber 20. FIG. 2 further shows an upstream sealing land 30 and a downstream sealing land 32 joined by a reduced-diameter waist 34 in the fill position, and a one-way outlet valve 38.
8	
9	The dose chamber 20 is cylindrical. The concentrate port 22 is a radial port through the wall of the metering sleeve 18 and is connected in use to a concentrate source. The carrier-liquid admission port 24 passes through the wall of the metering sleeve 18 at an axial position downstream of the concentrate port 22, and admits carrier liquid to the dose chamber 20. The metering sleeve 18 further defines a flush bypass 26 that opens downstream of the dose chamber 20.
10	
11	A piston 28 is axially slidable in the dose chamber 20 between a fill position and a discharge position. The upstream sealing land 30 and the downstream sealing land 32 are axially spaced from one another on the piston 28 and are joined by the reduced-diameter waist 34. Each sealing land bears on the wall of the dose chamber 20, while the waist 34 stands clear of that wall. A piston rod 36 extends from the piston 28 along the axis of the dose chamber 20 and is arranged to be driven through a stroke and a return stroke. The one-way outlet valve 38 is arranged to pass liquid from the dose chamber 20 toward the outlet 16 and to prevent flow in the opposite direction.
12	
13	In the fill position the waist 34 connects the concentrate port 22 to the dose chamber 20, and the upstream sealing land 30 and the downstream sealing land 32 isolate the carrier-liquid admission port 24 from the concentrate port 22. Concentrate accordingly passes from the concentrate source through the concentrate port 22 into the dose chamber 20 to form a measured volume of concentrate, the extent of which is fixed by the travel then permitted to the piston 28. Throughout the fill position the carrier-liquid path is closed to the concentrate, because the downstream sealing land 32 overlies the carrier-liquid admission port 24 while the upstream sealing land 30 closes the dose chamber 20 on the other side of the waist 34.
14	
15	Movement of the piston 28 toward the discharge position closes the concentrate port 22 before the downstream sealing land 32 uncovers the carrier-liquid admission port 24. The upstream sealing land 30 arrives at the concentrate port 22 and shuts it while the downstream sealing land 32 is still overlying the carrier-liquid admission port 24. Only after that has happened does continued travel of the piston 28 carry the downstream sealing land 32 clear of the carrier-liquid admission port 24. Carrier liquid then enters through the carrier-liquid admission port 24 behind the measured volume of concentrate in the dose chamber 20 and expels the measured volume through the one-way outlet valve 38 toward the outlet 16, where it joins the main flow.

In the following description, the terms upstream and downstream refer to the direction of travel of the carrier liquid from the inlet toward the outlet, and the terms axial and radial refer to the axis along which the piston slides.

FIG. 1 shows an inline liquid metering valve 10 having a cylindrical housing 12 with an inlet 14 at one axial end and an outlet 16 at the opposite axial end, a metering sleeve 18 fixed within the housing 12, a cartridge 64 retained in the housing 12 by a threaded end cap 66, and a transparent window 52 in the housing 12.

The inline liquid metering valve 10 is connected in a line that already carries a flowing carrier liquid. Carrier liquid enters at the inlet 14, passes along the housing 12, and leaves at the outlet 16. That flow is the main flow into which each dose of concentrate is delivered, and it is also the only liquid used to rinse the valve. The metering sleeve 18 is spaced radially inward from the inner surface of the housing 12 over part of its length.

FIG. 2 shows the metering sleeve 18 defining a dose chamber 20, a concentrate port 22 opening into the dose chamber 20 and a carrier-liquid admission port 24 opening into the dose chamber 20. FIG. 2 further shows an upstream sealing land 30 and a downstream sealing land 32 joined by a reduced-diameter waist 34 in the fill position, and a one-way outlet valve 38.

The dose chamber 20 is cylindrical. The concentrate port 22 is a radial port through the wall of the metering sleeve 18 and is connected in use to a concentrate source. The carrier-liquid admission port 24 passes through the wall of the metering sleeve 18 at an axial position downstream of the concentrate port 22, and admits carrier liquid to the dose chamber 20. The metering sleeve 18 further defines a flush bypass 26 that opens downstream of the dose chamber 20.

A piston 28 is axially slidable in the dose chamber 20 between a fill position and a discharge position. The upstream sealing land 30 and the downstream sealing land 32 are axially spaced from one another on the piston 28 and are joined by the reduced-diameter waist 34. Each sealing land bears on the wall of the dose chamber 20, while the waist 34 stands clear of that wall. A piston rod 36 extends from the piston 28 along the axis of the dose chamber 20 and is arranged to be driven through a stroke and a return stroke. The one-way outlet valve 38 is arranged to pass liquid from the dose chamber 20 toward the outlet 16 and to prevent flow in the opposite direction.

In the fill position the waist 34 connects the concentrate port 22 to the dose chamber 20, and the upstream sealing land 30 and the downstream sealing land 32 isolate the carrier-liquid admission port 24 from the concentrate port 22. Concentrate accordingly passes from the concentrate source through the concentrate port 22 into the dose chamber 20 to form a measured volume of concentrate, the extent of which is fixed by the travel then permitted to the piston 28. Throughout the fill position the carrier-liquid path is closed to the concentrate, because the downstream sealing land 32 overlies the carrier-liquid admission port 24 while the upstream sealing land 30 closes the dose chamber 20 on the other side of the waist 34.

Movement of the piston 28 toward the discharge position closes the concentrate port 22 before the downstream sealing land 32 uncovers the carrier-liquid admission port 24. The upstream sealing land 30 arrives at the concentrate port 22 and shuts it while the downstream sealing land 32 is still overlying the carrier-liquid admission port 24. Only after that has happened does continued travel of the piston 28 carry the downstream sealing land 32 clear of the carrier-liquid admission port 24. Carrier liquid then enters through the carrier-liquid admission port 24 behind the measured volume of concentrate in the dose chamber 20 and expels the measured volume through the one-way outlet valve 38 toward the outlet 16, where it joins the main flow.

The axial ordering of the faces of the upstream sealing land 30 and the downstream sealing land 32 relative to the edges of the concentrate port 22 and the carrier-liquid admission port 24 is chosen so that the concentrate port 22 is closed at every position of the piston 28 at which the carrier-liquid admission port 24 is open. There is accordingly no position of the piston 28 at which the concentrate source communicates directly with the carrier-liquid path. The separation of the two liquids is a property of the geometry of the piston 28 and the metering sleeve 18. It does not depend on the order in which external commands are given, on any control signal, or on the correct operation of a separately actuated shut-off element. A slow stroke, an interrupted stroke, or a stroke reversed part way through cannot open both ports at once, because the port that must close does so at an earlier point on the same continuous path of travel than the point at which the other port opens.

FIG. 4 shows an index collar 40 having a helical cam groove 42 engaged by a follower pin 44 carried by the piston rod 36, three selectable axial stop faces 46, a spring-biased detent 48 engaging one of three detent recesses 50, and three dose setting numerals 54.

The index collar 40 surrounds the metering sleeve 18. Each full stroke of the piston 28 draws the follower pin 44 along the helical cam groove 42 and turns the index collar 40 by one increment, so that the index collar 40 advances by itself as the valve is used and needs no separate indexing drive.

The three axial stop faces 46 are carried by the index collar 40 at different axial positions. The stop face presented by the current increment of rotation limits the travel of the piston 28 and thereby sets the dose volume, so that the three axial stop faces 46 correspond to three dose volumes. The spring-biased detent 48 engages one of the three detent recesses 50 to retain the selected setting until the index collar 40 is next indexed.

The transparent window 52 in the housing 12 shows one of the three dose setting numerals 54 carried by the index collar 40. The dose setting numeral presented at the transparent window 52 is the one associated with the axial stop face then limiting the travel of the piston 28, so that the dose setting is mechanically visible without electronics. What is seen at the transparent window 52 is the position of the mechanism itself rather than a stored value, so the displayed setting cannot disagree with the volume that the valve will deliver.

FIG. 3 shows the piston 28 during the return stroke toward the fill position, with a flexible lip 56, the follower pin 44 holding a flush poppet 58 open, an annular rinse channel 60, two radial rinse openings 62 of which one is directed across the concentrate port 22, and the flush bypass 26.

The flexible lip 56 is carried on the upstream sealing land 30 and bears on the wall of the dose chamber 20. As the return stroke begins, the flexible lip 56 wipes the wall of the dose chamber 20 and carries the film of concentrate remaining on that wall ahead of it, so that the rinse which follows is presented with a wetted surface rather than with standing liquid.

The annular rinse channel 60 lies between an outer surface of the metering sleeve 18 and an inner surface of the housing 12, and is supplied with carrier liquid from the inlet 14. The two radial rinse openings 62 pass through the wall of the metering sleeve 18 and connect the annular rinse channel 60 to the dose chamber 20. One of the two radial rinse openings 62 is directed across the concentrate port 22 and the other is directed across the one-way outlet valve 38. Those are the two surfaces on which concentrate is otherwise retained after a dose, the first because concentrate stands in the mouth of the port and the second because concentrate is the last liquid to pass the one-way outlet valve 38.

The flush poppet 58 is normally closed and is connected to the flush bypass 26. Near the end of the return stroke, the follower pin 44 reaches the flush poppet 58 and opens it. Carrier liquid then flows from the inlet 14 through the annular rinse channel 60, through the two radial rinse openings 62 across the concentrate port 22 and the one-way outlet valve 38, and through the flush bypass 26 to the outlet 16. The rinse liquid therefore reaches the outlet 16, as the dose does, and is carried away in the main flow.

The flush poppet 58 closes before the waist 34 reconnects the concentrate port 22 to the dose chamber 20. The concentrate port 22 is closed throughout the interval in which the annular rinse channel 60 communicates with the flush bypass 26, so that carrier liquid at the pressure of the main line is never presented to an open concentrate port 22 and cannot be driven back toward the concentrate source. Only when the flush poppet 58 has closed does the continuing return of the piston 28 bring the waist 34 back into register with the concentrate port 22, at which point the dose chamber 20 is charged again for the next dose.

Because the follower pin 44 that opens the flush poppet 58 is carried by the piston rod 36, the rinse occurs once for every dose and at the same point in every cycle. It is not a separate operation, it needs no command, and it cannot be omitted while the valve continues to be used. The rinse also occurs while the concentrate port 22 is shut and after the wall of the dose chamber 20 has been wiped, so that it removes a film with clean carrier liquid instead of diluting a standing charge of concentrate.

The cartridge 64 contains the piston 28, the metering sleeve 18, the one-way outlet valve 38 and the flush poppet 58, and is removable from the housing 12 as a unit. Removing the threaded end cap 66 withdraws the cartridge 64 from the housing 12 along the axis of the dose chamber 20 without disturbing the connections at the inlet 14 and the outlet 16, so that the cartridge 64 is replaced as a unit while the housing 12 remains in the line.

In use, carrier liquid flows through the housing 12 from the inlet 14 to the outlet 16. With the piston 28 in the fill position, concentrate is admitted through the concentrate port 22 and past the waist 34 into the dose chamber 20 to form a measured volume, the upstream sealing land 30 and the downstream sealing land 32 isolating the carrier-liquid admission port 24 from the concentrate port 22. The piston 28 is then advanced toward the discharge position so as to close the concentrate port 22 and thereafter to uncover the carrier-liquid admission port 24 with the downstream sealing land 32. Carrier liquid is admitted through the carrier-liquid admission port 24 behind the measured volume and expels the measured volume through the one-way outlet valve 38 toward the outlet 16. The extent of the travel available to the piston 28, and therefore the measured volume, is fixed by the selected one of the three axial stop faces 46.

The piston 28 is then returned toward the fill position. During the return, the flexible lip 56 on the upstream sealing land 30 wipes the wall of the dose chamber 20, and the follower pin 44 carried by the piston rod 36 opens the normally closed flush poppet 58. Carrier liquid flows through the annular rinse channel 60 between the metering sleeve 18 and the housing 12, through the two radial rinse openings 62 in the metering sleeve 18 across the concentrate port 22 and the one-way outlet valve 38, and through the flush bypass 26 that opens downstream of the dose chamber 20 to the outlet 16. The flush poppet 58 is closed before the waist 34 reconnects the concentrate port 22 to the dose chamber 20. Over the same full stroke, the follower pin 44 travelling in the helical cam groove 42 turns the index collar 40 by one increment, the spring-biased detent 48 enters the next of the three detent recesses 50, and the dose setting numeral then presented at the transparent window 52 shows the setting that will govern the next dose. The valve is thereby left charged, rinsed and set, ready for the following cycle.

The foregoing description sets out embodiments of the invention. A skilled reader may make changes of detail to the described embodiments without departing from the scope of the claims that follow.

SOURCE-FIDELITY PREFLIGHT v9 (section-line consistency) — p12, "Self-Flushing Inline Liquid Metering Valve With Indexed Dose Selection".

SOURCES. input/disclosure.md and the single USER turn in input/conversation.md are substantively identical; there is no corrective, narrowing, auditing or rejecting USER turn, so the whole disclosure text is affirmative support. input/brief.md was relied on only for formalities: title (matches 01-title.md verbatim), applicant/inventor, "Not applicable." in 02 and 03, apparatus+method claim classes, the no-means-plus-function instruction (none used), and the six preserved terms (metering sleeve, dose chamber, flush bypass, index collar, flush poppet, annular rinse channel — all present and used consistently). review/previous-qa.md was treated as context only.

LEDGER — CLAIMS. Every limitation of claims 1–20 traces to affirmative inventor text. Claim 1 maps clause by clause to disclosure ¶2–¶4 (housing with inlet and outlet; sleeve fixed within the housing defining dose chamber, concentrate port, carrier-liquid admission port, flush bypass opening downstream; "an annular rinse channel between the sleeve and housing"; "two radial rinse openings"; piston with two axially spaced lands and reduced-diameter waist; "a follower pin carried by the piston rod"; "a one-way outlet valve"; "a normally closed flush poppet"; fill-position isolation; close-before-uncover ordering; poppet opened by the pin on the return and closing "before the waist reconnects the concentrate port"). Claims 2–12 and 14–20 trace to the disclosed species (rinse openings "directed across the concentrate port and the one-way outlet valve"; "a flexible lip on the upstream sealing land first wipes the dose-chamber wall"; "The ordering of the port edges and lands prevents..."; "helical cam groove engaged by a follower pin"; "Three selectable axial stop faces... set three dose volumes by limiting piston travel"; "A spring-biased detent engages one of three recesses"; "A transparent window in the housing shows one of three reference numerals carried on the collar"; the cartridge/threaded end cap sentences; "a cylindrical housing with an inlet at one axial end and an outlet at the opposite axial end"). Claim 1's genus wording ("at least one rinse opening", housing not recited as cylindrical) rests on disclosed species and is claim scope, not a fidelity gap. Claims 4 and 16 ("the concentrate port is closed throughout an interval in which the annular rinse channel communicates with the flush bypass") are a fair restatement of "The flush poppet closes before the waist reconnects the concentrate port". Renaming the collar's "reference numerals" to "dose setting numerals 54" avoids collision with drawing numerals and preserves the disclosed meaning.

LEDGER — DESCRIPTION AND FIGURES. The added axial relationships I traced closely all follow necessarily from the disclosure and are therefore not reported: the admission port lying downstream of the concentrate port and being overlain by the downstream land in the fill position follow from "both lands isolate the carrier-liquid path" plus "before the downstream land uncovers the carrier-liquid admission port"; the upstream land being the land that shuts the concentrate port follows from the disclosed order (an upstream stroke would uncover the admission port before closing the concentrate port); the concentrate port being covered during the rinse follows from the poppet closing "before the waist reconnects" it. The annulus being open at both ends is required by the disclosed inline main flow and is the fix directed by the previous review; I did not re-open it. Six description/summary statements state results, purposes or exclusivities that no USER passage affirms; they are reported as minor items with delete-only fixes.

NUMERALS. All 29 entries in draft/numerals.md trace to named inventor structures, each numeral means exactly one thing, each is used in 08-detailed-description.md, and the four per-figure lists in the description match the briefs exactly (FIG. 1: 10/12/14/16/18/52/64/66; FIG. 2: 18/20/22/24/30/32/34/38; FIG. 3: 22/26/28/44/56/58/60/62; FIG. 4: 36/40/42/44/46/48/50/54). Their union covers all 29 with none orphaned. Upstream/downstream usage (inlet left, land 30 left, land 32 right) is consistent across all four briefs and the text.

SECTION LINES. No view is designated as taken along a section line of another view, so there is no repeated designation to reconcile. FIGS. 2 and 3 are enlargements, and the view sentences ("of FIG. 1", "with the piston in the fill position", "during the return stroke... with the flush poppet held open") appear identically in 07-drawings.md, fig-02.md/fig-03.md and the description's view sentences at lines 7 and 27. FIG. 4's designation "fragmentary side view of the index collar and the parts that set and retain the dose" is identical in 07-drawings.md, fig-04.md and line 19. This check is clean.

DEPICTION CONVENTIONS ACCEPTED. Ball-and-seat for the one-way outlet valve, head-and-stem for the flush poppet, tubular stubs for inlet and outlet, the concentrate-source tube, the ball-and-broken-spring detent, and the blank patches for the dose setting numerals are each called "shown schematically", add no technical function, and are matched by shape-neutral claim and description wording. No "by way of example", "any closed outline" or similar sentence was added to the application text to justify a visual choice.

NO DRAFTING DEBRIS. No note, placeholder, open question, instruction, unresolved alternative or internal comment remains in any draft or figure file. The abstract is one paragraph of about 140 words.

FINDINGS: 7. One major internal-logic conflict: FIG. 1 confines the piston rod to the sleeve bore with the sleeve's left end against the end cap, leaving the follower pin 44 no route to the flush poppet stem (FIG. 3) or the cam groove of the collar surrounding the sleeve (FIG. 4), and directly contradicting FIG. 3's "past the sleeve's left end". Five minor fidelity items are added results/purposes with delete-only fixes. One minor formality: the detailed description discusses FIG. 4 before FIG. 3, out of the order given in the Brief Description. Every fix is a local, filing-clean edit; none adds structure, a speculative shape or an optional embodiment.

findings.title: FIG. 1 confines the piston rod to the sleeve bore and seats the sleeve end on the end cap, leaving follower pin 44 no route to the flush poppet or the index collar shown in FIGS. 3 and 4
findings.where: figures/fig-01.md (shaft sentence in the end-cap bullet; cartridge bullet); cf. figures/fig-03.md (piston bullet) and figures/fig-04.md (piston rod bullet)
findings.detail: FIG. 1 states that the rod runs inside the sleeve and that the sleeve's left end face bears on the end cap, so nothing carried by the rod can reach outside the sleeve. FIG. 3, an enlargement of the same left-hand region, requires the opposite: the shaft passes beyond the sleeve's left end and the pin projects upward from it into the annular gap to lift the poppet stem. FIG. 4 likewise requires the pin to project radially into the cam groove of a collar that surrounds the sleeve. The same numbered parts (piston rod 36, follower pin 44) therefore have incompatible routes in the three briefs. The disclosure requires the pin to act outside the sleeve ('An index collar surrounds the metering sleeve and has a helical cam groove engaged by a follower pin carried by the piston rod'), so FIG. 1 is the brief that must change; the end-face contact it asserts is itself an unstated detail, the disclosure saying only that the cartridge 'is retained by a threaded end cap'.

A short follower pin projects radially from the end of the shaft, its outer end sitting within the narrow band of the groove."
